page.layout: Two printed columns of text and notes on one page: a narrow column of marginal notes in the left margin, and the main text block to its right. Running head at top; page number 476 at top. No footnotes and no catchword.

main_text.l: Quod si vero quis obiiciat, contactum secundum Philo-
sophos esse duplicem, vnum corporalem, alterum virtualem;
& hunc posteriorem etiam competere substantiis
incorporeis. Respondeo, contactum virtualem attribui
substantiis incorporeis non proprie, sed Metaphorice;
ideoq; obiectionem illam nullam vim habere thesin no-
stram infringendi, quæ loquitur de contiguitate propria.

l.i: 15 An omne corpus per se habeat sex positionum

main_text.l: Ensis problem. est, an omne corpus talem ordinem,
situm ac distantiam partium habeat, vt per se alia sit
superior, alia inferior, alia dextra, alia sinistra, alia an-
terior, alia posterior. Etsi vero nonnulli Philosophi
olim fuerunt, qui omni corpori sex positionum differen-
tias attribuendas esse censuerunt; tum quod omne est
extensum in longum, latum & profundum; tum, quod su-
perius est principium longitudinis; dextrum latitudinis,
anterius profunditatis; tamen hanc sententiam reiicit
Aristot. lib. 2 de cœlo, cap. 2. Ait enim expresse, non esse
quærendum in omni corpore superius & inferius, de-
xtrum & sinistrum, anterius & posterius; sed in corpori-
bus animatis, quæ principium motus in seipsis habent,
iisque non omnibus, sed illis duntaxat quæ sunt perfecta:
Hinc affert, quibusdam animalibus inesse omnes
sex positionum differentias, quibusdam nonnullas,
nempe quatuor; plantis vero tantum duas, superam & infe-
ram videlicet. Unde porro colligitur, corpora inanimata
non habere per se sex positionum differentias, nempe
neque superiorem, neque inferiorem, neque dextram,
neque sinistram, neque anteriorem, neque posteriorem;
sed tantum per accidens, quatenus vel ad nos referuntur:
vel ad similitudinem nostri ab artificibus efformantur,
vel ad positum cœli & terræ considerantur.

l.i: 16 An corpus possit naturaliter transmutari in non corpus,

main_text.l: Ensis problematis est, utrum[?] virtute vllius creatu-
ræ subsistantia corporea possit converti in incorpoream, aut
ex incorporea substantia fieri. Ac veritas quidem thesis
negantis probari potest his argumentis: Primo, quia
solius Dei proprium est, sicut ex nihilo aliquid efficere,
& ex aliquo nihil; ita ex non corpore, efficere corpus,
aut

page.notes: The first letter of "Ensis" (line beginning "Ensus problem.") is a large initial E, joined to the word. Read as "Ensis" with a plain s. The word "virtute" in the sentence beginning "Ensis problematis est" is printed as "virum"; I read it as "utrum" with [?] because the first letter is unclear. The thesis numbers 15 and 16 are numbered theses, so they are paragraphs in italic, not headings. The marginal notes are in the left margin, and each stands beside the line where it sits. The printed hyphens in "nega-tiua", "ne-gante", "creatu-ræ" are kept as printed. The bottom-left faint mark and the "Digitized by Google" banner at the foot are not transcribed. The paragraph beginning "Primo" continues onto the next page.
